newsitem.title: EGYPT: YEAREND - Mideast privatisation - More promises than sales.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Mideast privatisation - More promises than sales.

text.p: Privatisation may have been one of the buzzwords at Middle East economic conferences in 1996 but in the real world the action lagged far behind the promises.
Even in Egypt, which changed into a higher gear after years of hesitation, brokers still take with a pinch of salt ministerial statements about the government's intentions.

In some countries the governments put the brake on privatisation for a host of reasons -- political upheaval, problems finding strategic investors, worries about the possible loss of jobs and doubts about the transparency of operations.
In Kuwait, for example, the state sold shares worth $224 million in 1996, against $870 million in 1995, largely because the opposition-dominated parliament demanded strict rules.
Promises have been lavish all round and, in economies open to foreign portfolio investment, they have persuaded foreign funds to take privatisation more seriously than ever before.

Egypt's privatisation boss, Public Enterprise Minister Atef Obeid, for instance, said in September he would sell off shares on the stock exchange at the rate of one firm a week for the rest of this year. In practice, only two tranches have reached the market.
In Israel, which has special problems of its own, the government is promising a "comprehensive privatisation programme" by the end of this month.
FEW PUBLIC COMPANIES FOR SALE

But their problem is to find buyers when the local stock market is in bad shape. Foreigners might also be hesitant to invest in Israel when so much doubt surrounds the future of peace talks between the Jewish state and its Arab neighbours.

In Tunisia, often portrayed as one of the most liberal economies in the region, Economic Development Minister Taoufik Baccar said in October that the state would sell another 15 companies by the end of the year. Only one small company has gone on offer so far.
Turkey's target for this year was to sell assets worth $2 billion, but by July it had clocked up only $292 million and the total for the year will be no more than $500 million.
In Jordan, most aspects of the economic reforms promised by the International Monetary Fund have been going through but so far not a single public sector company has gone private.
Even in countries where the pace did pick up in 1996, the governments have sold off only the tip of the iceberg.
Many governments hold vast portfolios of assets they acquired in the days when the state led the way to industrialisation and when foreign investment was suspect.
Economists say some state companies in formerly socialist countries such as Egypt may never find buyers because they are overstaffed and equipped with antiquated machinery.

"At the bottom of the pile there's an awful lot of rubbish. They will find it harder and harder to sell as they work their way down the list," said a foreign economist close to Egypt's economic liberalisation programme.

Obeid, the Egyptian minister, had a portfolio of 314 companies and in the last three years has sold some shares in several dozen of them. Even where the state has sold shares, it has rarely given up majority control.
The Moroccan government, in a programme started in 1994, has a list of 114 companies slated for privatisation by 1998. So far 27 companies and 18 hotels have gone private.
Tunisia, by crude numbers one of the most advanced along the road to privatisation, has sold 60 out of 400 state companies. At the current rate it will take many years to sell the rest.
WORLD BANK, IMF WANT SMALLER PUBLIC SECTOR

Economists say that in their programmes some Middle East governments appear to be responding, at least in part, to the ideology of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), both of which are pressing for a smaller public sector.
In Egypt the quicker pace of privatisation this year helped break a deadlock in talks with the IMF. After an agreement with the IMF in October, the Paris Club waived $4 billion in debt.

The World Bank is pressing Tunisia to sell off companies, and it believes the Turkish government cannot meet its 1997 budget targets without what it called "effective and speedy implementation of the privatisation programme".

"Foreign lobbying has been a factor almost everywhere. The Middle East doesn't have a Margaret Thatcher -- a politician ideologically committed to privatisation and willing to push it through against all the odds," said the foreign economist close to Egyptian privatisation.
The Gulf states, rich with oil and relatively immune from foreign financial pressures, have not as a group been among the pioneers in the field.
Analysts say the Gulf governments will find it difficult to wean their people from their generous welfare system and will avoid cutting public-sector jobs for political reasons.

The Bahraini government has sold only two companies, the government of the Abu Dhabi only one, and Oman has one private-sector investment in infrastructure, through a build-own-operate-transfer (BOT) arrangement at a power station. Qatar and Saudi Arabia have privatised nothing but may do so later.
